description_full: Delcath Systems, Inc., an interventional oncology company, focuses on the treatment of primary and metastatic liver cancers in the United States and Europe. The company's lead product candidate is HEPZATO KIT, a melphalan for injection/hepatic delivery system to administer high-dose chemotherapy to the liver while controlling systemic exposure and associated side effects. Its clinical development program for HEPZATO is the FOCUS clinical trial for patients with metastatic hepatic dominant Uveal Melanoma to investigate objective response rate in metastatic uveal melanoma. The company also provides HEPZATO as a stand-alone medical device under the CHEMOSAT Hepatic Delivery System trade name for Melphalan or CHEMOSAT for medical centers to treat a range of liver cancers in Europe. The company was founded in 1988 and is headquartered in Queensbury, New York.

financial_summary: Delcath Systems, Inc. is a small-cap healthcare business with a $518M market cap on $85M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +215% over the past three years and +48% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +1730.0pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at -80% against a 10% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests. Gross margins of 74% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $21M in free cash flow — roughly 25 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 8.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -16.0% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and stock-based comp at 28% of revenue is silent dilution an owner has to account for, and insiders hold 8.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
